chapter: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
title: Louis plays another trumpeter's horn
summary: Danny handed Louis a local trumpeter's horn and Louis tore up the house, but the owner scolded him; Milt and Danny try to name the player.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: So we sat down a while. So he said, "Let's play something!" But nothing happened. They're just going to wait and look at Louis, and talk about it. Then they asked him to play something. He ain't got no horn. So they had this band up, I forget which -- another band was playing. But we had blown them out, so they were just around there. And they had this little trumpeter, a little dark trumpet player, Swift, or Swaft...Swift...
No, not Bob. It was another little dark cat, very evil(?). I can't think of his name. So I'm sitting...
No. He could play. But he wasn't so fond of Louis, because Louis...
He wasn't a hunchback, was he? There was a guy named Mitch who had a hunchback.
You almost said it. Not (?), but a little cat. Looked something like Shad Collins. He had a name around Chicago.
It wasn't Tick Gray? Tick Gray.
Yeah, Tick, he was a little guy...

Well... So they kept begging Louis. So I'm by the bandstand, sitting up by the bandstand, looking at him, observing everything. And I said, 'Give him that horn!' I gave him the horn, and it ended up Louis and the band got on this thing...got around there, and they started playing. So Louis played 'When You're Smiling,' I think. Man, he just tore up the house in pieces, boy. People screaming. Then he played another one. And he was fingering the horn and looking at the horn like it was his
horn, you know, with (?) the number he played. So he got through (?) the horn and put it back.

Then we got off intermission. This cat come up on the stand and told me, "Who the hell gave you permission to give Louis Armstrong my horn? I don't let nobody play my horn. Don't never do that no more." He's getting ready to fight me. "Don't never give nobody..." I said, "But that was Louis." "I don't give a goddamn who it was. I don't let nobody put their lips on my horn." So I felt real bad, you know, you know, because I had no business doing that. But who the hell would think a son-of-a-bitch who was this good blowing his horn.
